Original fixtures check a MacPherson mechanism against closed-form lower-arm motion, upright orientation and telescoping length through compression/rebound/return sweeps. Further cases check steering with three preserved lengths and a top point on the upright axis, rigid-frame covariance, an analytic Jacobian against central differences with a noncoincident strut attachment, singular/collapsed/reversed axes, unreachable commands and failed-solve immutability. The source adapter rejects wrong types and each missing required point. The CLI fixture now checks both DWB and STRUT reports through the reader/adapter/solver, retaining unchanged source bytes. The existing DWB analytical and local-source checks pass after sharing the Newton iteration.

Local STRUT checks covered 81 cases on the front suspensions of BMW M3 E30, BMW 1M and BMW M3 E92: travel from -40 to +40 mm in 10 mm increments, each with -2/0/+2 mm source-X steering-anchor displacement. A separate Python calculation expanded the returned quaternions and directly checked three source distances, top-to-axis perpendicular error, positive axial length and extension. Maximum length errors were 2.532e-11, 2.878e-11 and 2.999e-11 m respectively; maximum perpendicular errors were 4.016e-12, 5.421e-12 and 3.164e-12 m. All cases converged within four updates. The earlier 81 DWB source cases were also rerun successfully. These are raw-design constraint checks, not measurements of original-game wheel motion, suspension forces or performance.

The current Windows ordinary Rust test total is 143; the eleven explicit GPU and five window tests retain their separate scope. Full source-frame/setup mapping, physical chassis coupling, native wheel animation and original-game kinematics validation remain work ahead.

Suspension differential validation

Six original Rust kernel fixtures check closed-form parallel-wishbone and telescoping-strut velocities, all four differential columns against central pose differences, point-force torque and virtual power, ideal held force/moment balance and independently reconstructed rod/top reactions. Additional cases within these fixtures check rigid-frame rotation/translation covariance, mismatched/unconverged poses, invalid rates/points, excessive load amplification and map immutability. The CLI fixture covers both topologies, explicit rates/loads, report metadata and malformed/duplicate options with no partial JSON output. Together these add seven tests to the ordinary Windows total of 143; formatting and warning-free Clippy also pass.

Local source checks covered both axles of BMW M3 E30, Ferrari 458 and SDK Formula K at -30/0/+30 mm travel and +2 mm source-X rack displacement: 18 cases. Each used explicit synthetic rates [0.17, 0.025, -0.012, 0.009] m/s and a synthetic force [120, 2300, -300] N with torque [40, -15, 25] N m about the upright origin. An independent Python calculation compared velocities with solved poses at +/-0.001 seconds, expanded quaternions separately and reconstructed support moments from source anchors, rod directions and the ideal STRUT top reaction.

Across these cases the maximum origin-velocity difference was 6.787e-9 m/s and angular-velocity difference 8.047e-8 rad/s. Virtual-power discrepancy stayed below 1.288e-13 W, force-balance residual below 4.548e-13 N, and torque balance/reconstructed support/frame-moment errors below 5.685e-14 N m. These are numerical consistency results for raw source geometry and ideal massless supports under supplied loads. They do not validate original-game force transfer, tyre/spring laws, chassis dynamics or driving. Raw game/SDK records and temporary reports remain excluded from Git.

Reproducible examples

Tests use small original fixtures generated in temporary directories, including complete original KN5 structures and explicitly header-only fixtures for the lightweight inspector. Do not add copied cars, tracks, textures, audio, or SDK archives to the repository. A parser change should include a minimal example proving the new behavior and invalid input that must be diagnosed.
